facts.statement: Nanotyrannus lancensis specimens are reported to have 15-16 teeth on the upper jaw and 16-18 on the lower jaw, while adult Tyrannosaurus rex has 11-12 upper and 12-14 lower teeth.
facts.quote: Specimens referred to N. lancensis have 15-16 teeth on each side of the maxilla (upper jaw) and 16-18 teeth on each side of the dentary (lower jaw), whereas adult T. rex specimens had 11–12 tooth positions in the upper jaw and 12–14 in the lower.

facts.statement: Tsujihi and colleagues noted that tooth count varies significantly between individuals of the same age in Tyrannosaurus and Gorgosaurus, suggesting it may not be strictly linked to growth.
facts.quote: These researchers also noted, however, that both Tyrannosaurus and Gorgosaurus show significant differences in tooth count between individuals of the same age group, and that tooth count may vary on an individual basis unrelated to growth.

facts.statement: A small foramen on the quadratojugal bone is cited as a difference supporting the validity of Nanotyrannus lancensis.
facts.quote: Another difference cited in support of the validity of N. lancensis is the presence of a small foramen on the quadratojugal.

facts.statement: A 2020 study by Woodward and colleagues concluded that Nanotyrannus specimens are ontogenetically immature and likely belong to Tyrannosaurus rex.
facts.quote: A 2020 study by Holly N. Woodward and colleagues indicated that the specimens referred to Nanotyrannus are ontogenetically immature and found it probable that these specimens belonged to Tyrannosaurus rex.

facts.statement: In 2015, Yun claimed that all distinguishing features of Nanotyrannus were due to individual variation, ontogeny, or taphonomic distortion.
facts.quote: Yun (2015) claimed that all of the differences used to distinguish Nanotyrannus were individually or ontogenetically variable features, or the products of taphonomic distortion of the bones.

facts.statement: In 2024, Longrich and Saitta suggested Nanotyrannus is a distinct taxon potentially outside Tyrannosauridae based on morphology, ontogeny, and phylogeny.
facts.quote: In 2024, Nicholas Longrich and Evan T. Saitta re-examined the holotype and referred specimens of Nanotyrannus. Based on several factors, including differences in morphology, ontogeny, and phylogeny, Longrich and Saitta suggested that Nanotyrannus is a distinct taxon that may fall outside of Tyrannosauridae, based on some of their phylogenetic analyses.

facts.statement: In June 2025, Voris et al. suggested Longrich and Saitta's 2024 placement of Nanotyrannus was due to immaturity-related scoring and data issues, supporting the view that it is a juvenile T. rex.
facts.quote: Voris et al. (June 2025) suggested that the scoring of Nanotyrannus in a more basal position by Longrich & Saitta (2024) may have been caused by "scoring characteristics related to immaturity" and problematic data sets, supporting the previous interpretation that Nanotyrannus represents a juvenile T. rex.

facts.statement: In June 2025, Gregory S. Paul supported a basal eutyrannosaurian position for Nanotyrannus as part of his "multiple small taxa hypothesis" for theropod diversity.
facts.quote: Later in June 2025, Gregory S. Paul also supported a basal eutyrannosaurian (non-tyrannosaurid) position for Nanotyrannus, emphasizing the validity and distinction of this genus as part of his preferred "multiple small taxa hypothesis" (MSTH) for theropod diversity in the Hell Creek Formation.

facts.statement: Paul argued that N. lancensis is a wastebasket taxon comprising fossils of multiple taxa under his MSTH framework.
facts.quote: Based on the MSTH, Paul also argued for the validity of Stygivenator, a Hell Creek theropod known from a fragmentary skull, and claimed that N. lancensis has been treated as a wastebasket taxon that likely comprises fossils of multiple taxa.

facts.statement: In October 2025, Zanno and Napoli affirmed the validity of Nanotyrannus after re-examining the "Bloody Mary" specimen.
facts.quote: In October 2025, the validity of Nanotyrannus was affirmed in an extensive paper by Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli, in which the "Bloody Mary" specimen (NCSM 40000) was re-examined.

facts.statement: Zanno and Napoli concluded that traits like tooth count variation are due to individual variation rather than ontogenetic plasticity.
facts.quote: Furthermore, they concluded that many of the traits commonly cited as ontogenetically plastic (i.e. variations in tooth count) were subject instead to individual variation.

facts.statement: Zanno and Napoli noted that the sinus obliteration required for Nanotyrannus and T. rex to be the same taxon has no precedent in living amniotes.
facts.quote: Further, they noted that certain traits, such as the "obliteration and resorption of a sinus" which would be necessary for Nanotyrannus and Tyrannosaurus to represent the same taxon, have no precedent among living amniotes.

facts.statement: Zanno and Napoli cited larger arm, wrist, and hand bones in Nanotyrannus compared to Tyrannosaurus as a difference.
facts.quote: Bone proportions were another difference cited by Zanno and Napoli, as some of the arm, wrist, and hand bones of Nanotyrannus are larger than equivalent bones in Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Zanno and Napoli noted no known amniotes undergo absolute limb shrinkage, only proportional changes due to slower limb growth.
facts.quote: There are no amniotes known to the authors that undergo any degree of absolute limb shrinkage, merely instances where limbs grew slower than the rest of the body and became proportionally smaller.

facts.statement: Some paleontologists who previously questioned Nanotyrannus validity, including Thomas Carr, Steve Brusatte, and David Hone, accepted that the "Bloody Mary" specimen is a distinct species from Tyrannosaurus rex.
facts.quote: Authors who have authored papers questioning Nanotyrannus validity, such as Thomas Carr, Steve Brusatte and David Hone, accepted that the "Bloody Mary" specimen was a distinct species from Tyrannosaurus rex

facts.statement: Researchers concluded that the N. lancensis holotype belongs to a mature individual based on hyoid bone sampling.
facts.quote: After sampling the hyoids of the N. lancensis holotype, the researchers concluded that it belongs to a mature individual

facts.statement: Nanotyrannus was a mid-sized tyrannosauroid.
facts.quote: Nanotyrannus was a mid-sized tyrannosauroid

facts.quote: the accompanying press release noted that the animal would have reached approximately 17 ft long and weighed 1000 lb

facts.quote: The holotype skull (CMNH 7541) of Nanotyrannus measures 57.2 cm when measured from the anterior (front) tip of the premaxilla to the posterior (rear) tip of the quadrate

facts.statement: The prominent subnarial foramen along the ventral extremity of the premaxilla-maxilla contact point is absent in every specimen of Nanotyrannus.
facts.quote: this is absent in every specimen of Nanotyrannus

facts.statement: The basitubera of Nanotyrannus were strongly laterally expanded, suggesting the head could be strongly flexed sideways.
facts.quote: the basitubera (muscle attachment sites at the back of the head) of Nanotyrannus were strongly laterally expanded, suggesting that the head could be strongly flexed sideways

facts.statement: The lower jaw bone of Nanotyrannus has a rounded front edge.
facts.quote: The dentary of Nanotyrannus (the tooth-bearing bone of the lower jaw), has a rounded anterior margin.

facts.statement: The front upper teeth of Nanotyrannus lacked serrations, a trait shared with other tyrannosauroids like Moros and Timurlengia.
facts.quote: The premaxillary teeth of Nanotyrannus are distinct from those of other tyrannosauroids in that they were completely devoid of serrations, like Moros, Timurlengia, and Xiongguanlong

facts.statement: Each front upper jaw bone of Nanotyrannus held four chisel-shaped teeth.
facts.quote: Each premaxilla bore four chisel-shaped teeth.

facts.statement: The upper jaw bones of Nanotyrannus held between fifteen and seventeen teeth, with the holotype preserving fifteen.
facts.quote: The maxillae of Nanotyrannus have variable tooth counts: the holotype specimen preserves fifteen, NCSM 40000 has sixteen on the left maxilla and seventeen on the right maxilla, and N. lethaeus appears to have sixteen per maxilla.

facts.statement: The frontmost upper teeth of Nanotyrannus were small and resembled the front teeth, unlike in Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: Unlike Daspletosaurus, Tarbosaurus, and Tyrannosaurus, but like many other tyrannosauroids, the most anterior tooth of each maxilla was small and resembled those of the premaxillae.

facts.statement: The upper teeth of Nanotyrannus were ziphodont (serrated on the inner edge), unlike most tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: Unlike most tyrannosaurids, the maxillary teeth were ziphodont.

facts.statement: Nanotyrannus had sixteen to eighteen lower jaw teeth, more than any tyrannosaurid except Alioramus and Daspletosaurus.
facts.quote: Nanotyrannus has between sixteen and eighteen teeth per dentary, a higher count than in any tyrannosaurid except for Alioramus and Daspletosaurus.

facts.statement: Nanotyrannus had approximately twenty neck vertebrae and thirty-five tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: The vertebral column of Nanotyrannus appears to consist of twenty presacral vertebrae (those before the sacrum), and thirty-five caudal (tail) vertebrae.

facts.statement: The lower end of the upper arm bone in Nanotyrannus had five bumps, a feature not found in other eutyrannosaurs.
facts.quote: The distal (further from the body) end of the humerus (upper arm bone) of Nanotyrannus bears five tubercles, unlike other eutyrannosaurs.

facts.statement: Nanotyrannus had a two-fingered hand but retained a small bone from a third finger, similar to Gorgosaurus.
facts.quote: The manus was functionally didactyl (two-fingered), though it does retain the first phalanx (finger bone) of a vestigial third digit, as in Gorgosaurus

facts.statement: The first finger bone of Nanotyrannus was nearly twice as large as the equivalent bone in Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: The first phalanx of the first manual digit is nearly twice the size of that of the equivalent bone in Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Nanotyrannus had hind legs that were proportionally much longer than those of other eutyrannosaurs.
facts.quote: The hind limbs of Nanotyrannus are proportionally very long compared to those of other eutyrannosaurs.

facts.statement: The foot bones of the NCSM 40000 specimen of Nanotyrannus were almost as long as those of the largest Tyrannosaurus, despite the animal's smaller size.
facts.quote: Despite its body size being far smaller, the metatarsals of NCSM 40000 are almost as long as those of the very largest Tyrannosaurus specimens.

facts.statement: Adult N. lancensis likely weighed around 704 kg based on the Bloody Mary specimen.
facts.quote: El N. lancensis adulto pudo haber pesado alrededor de 704 kg, según el espécimen de Bloody Mary.

facts.statement: Adult N. lethaeus could have reached a body mass of approximately 1200 kg.
facts.quote: N. lethaeus, por su parte, era más grande; los individuos maduros pudieron haber alcanzado una masa corporal de aproximadamente 1200 kg.

facts.statement: Nanotyrannus measured about 5.5 meters long and 2 meters high, roughly one-third the size of Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: Solo medía alrededor de 5,5 metros de longitud y 2 de altura, un tercio del tamaño de Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Nanotyrannus had a flat, square skull about 60 cm long, sharp claws and teeth, and a heavy body.
facts.quote: En general tenía las características de cualquier tiranosáurido del Cretácico, una cabeza chata y cuadrada con un tamaño cercano a los 60 centímetros de largo, contaba con garras y dientes afilados, así como un cuerpo no liviano.

facts.statement: Unlike Tyrannosaurus, Nanotyrannus had a thin, low skull with small crests or horns just in front of the eyes.
facts.quote: A diferencia de Tyrannosaurus, Nanotyrannus tenía un cráneo delgado y bajo, y pequeñas crestas o cuernos justo delante de los ojos.

facts.statement: Bakker suggests that Nanotyrannus hunted in packs due to its weight and build.
facts.quote: Bakker sostiene que, debido a su peso y complexion, Nanotyrannus cazaba en manadas.

facts.statement: Teeth from multiple Nanotyrannus individuals have been found in herbivore bones.
facts.quote: Dientes de múltiples Nanotyrannus han sido encontrados en huesos de herbívoros.

facts.statement: Nanotyrannus had longer legs than contemporaries, suggesting it was a pursuit predator, and had larger forelimbs both absolutely and proportionally than its relatives.

facts.statement: While Nanotyrannus is the only definitive member of the clade Nanotyrannidae, a phylogenetic hypothesis suggests it descended from an Appalachian tyrannosaur lineage that migrated to Laramidia as the Western Interior Seaway regressed.

facts.statement: Scientists have primarily distinguished Nanotyrannus from Tyrannosaurus based on differences in the number of teeth.

facts.statement: Nanotyrannus lancensis had 14 to 15 teeth on each side of the upper jaw and 16 teeth on each side of the lower jaw.

facts.statement: The exact implications of the difference in tooth number between Nanotyrannus and Tyrannosaurus have been controversial.
facts.quote: Las implicaciones exactas de esta diferencia en el número de dientes ha sido controvertida.

facts.statement: Carr used data showing that tooth number decreased as Gorgosaurus libratus developed to support the hypothesis that Nanotyrannus lancensis is simply a juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex.

facts.statement: A 2006 discovery of a juvenile Tarbosaurus skull with the same tooth count as adults supports the view that Nanotyrannus is a distinct genus.
facts.quote: Un cráneo de un Tarbosaurus juvenil descubierto en 2006 exhibe el mismo número de dientes que los cráneos adultos de Tarbosaurus, apoyando la idea de que Nanotyrannus es un género diferente.

facts.statement: Supporters of Nanotyrannus validity cite the presence of a small foramen in the squamosal bone at the back corner of the skull as a distinguishing feature.
facts.quote: Otra diferencia citada por quienes apoyan la validez de N. lancensis es la presencia de un pequeño foramen, un agujero en el hueso cuadratoyugal, que está situado en la esquina posterior del cráneo.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the squamosal foramen is an individual variable or lost during maturation, as studies of other juvenile tyrannosaurs do not show an equivalent trait.
